messages.text: Our events table is 40 million rows and the dashboard query takes 11 seconds, which is past the point where anyone uses the dashboard.
Eleven seconds is a plan problem before it is a hardware problem. Get EXPLAIN ANALYZE on exactly the query the dashboard sends, not a simplified version of it.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a sequential scan filtering on tenant_id and created_at, even though there is an index on each of those columns separately.
Two single-column indexes cannot serve an equality plus a range on the same table cheaply. A composite index on tenant_id first, created_at second is what turns that into an index range scan.
Adding the composite index with created_at descending dropped the query to 90ms, from 11 seconds.
That is the expected shape: the planner now reads a contiguous range instead of filtering 40 million rows. Keep the descending order only if the dashboard always sorts newest first.
The write path got slower though. Inserts went from about 4k a second to 3.1k.
That is the cost of the extra index page writes. Judge it against what the read bought you rather than in isolation.
I'm keeping the composite index. The dashboard is read-mostly and the insert cost is acceptable for a quarter, but I want it re-measured if write volume grows.
Sensible, with a trigger to revisit. Write the threshold down or the review never happens.
The Lighthouse project datasource was the one that regressed worst, because it writes a row per event instead of batching them.
Row-per-event is the pattern that makes an index expensive. Batching collapses many index maintenance operations into one per statement.
I'll batch the inserts at 500 rows per statement and re-measure, and add a partial index on tenant_id where payload is null for the cleanup job.
Both are the right kind of change: one reduces index churn, the other keeps the cleanup job off the main index entirely.
Vacuum has not run on that table in six weeks because a long-running transaction has been holding it back.
